Claude.notes: The Kargu-2 opening, Project Maven arc, and Iron Dome precedent do genuine narrative work — each historical vignette creates exactly the problem the concept section then dissects. Advanced-level framing is spot-on: 'who bears responsibility' is the right cognitive question. Weakness is that insight is delivered authoritatively rather than earned by a protagonist — but that convention is defensible for a senior-analyst register.
Claude.topIssue: The narrative delivers insight to the learner rather than making the learner arrive at it; a handful of quiz items reward recall (year, number) more than judgment.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of LAWS, F2T2EA kill chain, meaningful human control, and loitering munition are technically clean. The 87% GPT-4 exploit finding is real (Fang et al., cs.CR arXiv 2404.08144) but is loosely dated as 'In 2023' when the work was published April 2024 using late-2023 experiments — precision matters when a technical claim is doing the argumentative lifting. Iron Dome interception counts and the ~1,000-centrifuge Stuxnet figure fall within the range in the technical literature.
Gemini.topIssue: The '87% one-day vulnerability' figure is attributed to '2023' but the Fang et al. paper landed in April 2024 — the year label deserves a fix or a citation.

Perplexity.notes: Real-world anchors are mostly recent: DoD 3000.09 updated 2023, ICRC 2021 position, Kargu-2 2020. The 'as of 2024' framing on CCW outcomes has a shelf life — CCW 2024/2025 sessions and the December 2023 UN General Assembly LAWS resolution (152-4-11) are not referenced and would sharpen the currency. The lab experience depends on the aesopacademy.org proxy being reachable; when offline the fallback replies degrade the applied-outcome value.
Perplexity.topIssue: The 'CCW has produced only non-binding principles' framing predates the December 2023 UNGA resolution 78/241 on LAWS — a citation would refresh the currency.

Claude.notes: The NGA imagery pipeline and IRA cases anchor the ISR argument well; the Robert Williams and ASPI Xinjiang examples do real work in bringing biometric and mass-surveillance abstractions down to concrete outcomes. Quizzes lean toward interpretation ('is significant because…', 'what is the intelligence value…') rather than raw recall — this is the strongest quiz set in the course so far.
Claude.topIssue: Character role for the learner is well framed in labs but 'insight-arrival' in the lesson body is still authorial — the DoD/NSA framing tells rather than shows the moral stakes.

Gemini.notes: FRVT, false-positive rate, and change detection are defined correctly. The reported '~50% SKYNET accuracy' figure derives from Christian Grothoff's 2016 Ars Technica critique of leaked NSA slides — the methodology of that critique is itself contested and the lesson does not flag that the number is a reviewer estimate rather than an NSA-published metric. The base-rate-fallacy framing is technically sound. IRA reach numbers align with Facebook's Senate testimony (126M) and the Mueller Report.
Gemini.topIssue: The '50%' SKYNET accuracy figure is presented as an established finding but is Grothoff's independent re-analysis of leaked slides — the epistemic status should be flagged.

Perplexity.notes: Currency is strong — Robert Williams (2020), OpenAI Feb 2024 threat report, IRA (2016-2018) all reflect the current understanding. Missing: mention of Clearview AI's post-2020 legal history (ICO fines, Illinois BIPA settlement), and the Meta/Threads-era influence-operation landscape. The lesson would benefit from an explicit 2025+ update on facial-recognition regulatory momentum (EU AI Act Article 5 came into force February 2025).
Perplexity.topIssue: No reference to the EU AI Act biometric prohibitions (effective February 2025) — a significant currency gap for a lesson on face-recognition governance.

Claude.notes: The AlphaCode-as-shellcode hook is a very sharp story move — it makes the offense-shift immediately legible without lecturing. Volt Typhoon and SolarWinds are load-bearing examples used well. The lab framings (CISA threat model, defensive UEBA design, attribution analysis) put the learner in real analyst roles, which is exactly what the applied-outcome dimension is asking for.
Claude.topIssue: Quiz set for L3 leans on named-actor recall (Volt Typhoon, HAFNIUM) more than on the harder judgment questions the lesson body actually earns.

Gemini.notes: Wiper malware, zero-day, UEBA and attribution concepts are technically clean. WormGPT's operational status is stated as if current — WormGPT's original developer shut it down in August 2023 after doxxing, and downstream 'WormGPT' branded tools since then are largely rebranded jailbroken commercial LLMs, which is worth flagging. Colonial Pipeline is correctly framed as ransomware without an AI role, but the label 'AI Gap' overstates the AI relevance to that specific incident.
Gemini.topIssue: The WormGPT reference presents an August-2023-shuttered tool as an ongoing category label — the ecosystem has moved to jailbroken commercial LLMs and the lesson should say so.

Perplexity.notes: Volt Typhoon (2023-2024), SolarWinds (2020), and DARPA AIxCC (Aug 2024 final) are all current and well-anchored. Missing: XZ Utils backdoor (March 2024), which is now the canonical supply-chain example alongside SolarWinds; and the ClickFix/AI-generated phishing wave documented by Proofpoint and Microsoft in 2024-2025. The lesson would benefit from a 2025 refresh acknowledging the AI-assisted social-engineering surge that changed defender priorities.
Perplexity.topIssue: Supply-chain section names SolarWinds and Microsoft Exchange but not XZ Utils (March 2024), which is now the reference case in this space.

Claude.notes: Best-in-course module. The October 7, 2022 BIS opening is a genuinely well-earned inciting incident — Nvidia's stock, ASML's EUV monopoly, the MacroPolo talent-flow finding all cohere into a single strategic argument. Density is right for Advanced. Labs put the learner in the Senate-advisor and diplomat seats, which is where this material has to be practiced to matter.
Claude.topIssue: Even here the protagonist role in the lesson body is 'you, the observer of geopolitics' rather than 'you, the decision-maker on a specific policy call' — the labs earn that, the story sections don't quite.

Gemini.notes: BIS controls, EUV monopoly (ASML), CHIPS Act, Entity List, Huawei Mate 60 Pro (SMIC 7nm) are all technically accurate at a level of detail rarely seen at this age band. The '3.5 trillion operations per second' phrasing is a plain-language rendering of the October 2022 IC/TC thresholds — the technical term is TPP (Total Processing Performance) with specific FLOPS × bit-length calculations; a footnote pointing to the actual EAR language would strengthen the citation trail.
Gemini.topIssue: The '3.5 trillion operations per second' threshold is a paraphrase of the EAR's actual TPP + performance-density formula — a real citation to §744.23 or the October 17, 2023 revision would help students who go looking.

Perplexity.notes: Currency is a strong point — Oct 2022 BIS, Oct 2023 BIS revision, Aug 2023 Huawei Mate 60 Pro, Bletchley Nov 2023 all reflect the current landscape. Missing: the November 2024 BIS supplemental controls, the AI Seoul Summit (May 2024) and Paris Summit (Feb 2025), and the DeepSeek R1 release (Jan 2025) which reset the compute-frontier debate. For a 'AI Geopolitics' lesson taught in 2026, DeepSeek's absence is the biggest currency gap in the whole course.
Perplexity.topIssue: The lesson makes no reference to DeepSeek R1 (Jan 2025), which materially changed the argument that export controls preserve US AI leadership.

Claude.notes: The START-I-in-Vienna-1991 opening is the sharpest analogy in the course: 'thermonuclear warheads cannot be e-mailed' does more argumentative work in one sentence than three paragraphs of exposition. Compute governance is the right central proposal to interrogate; the lab (Verification Design Challenge) puts the learner in the position of actually having to defend a mechanism, which is the whole point of the module.
Claude.topIssue: L4 (US-China dimension) leans heavily on the Nov 2023 San Francisco talks and doesn't yet incorporate the Sept 2024 Track 1.5 outcomes or the 2025 UN GA First Committee LAWS resolution — a currency refresh would strengthen the closer.

Gemini.notes: 'Meaningful human control' and 'compute governance' concepts are handled with the correct amount of definitional care — the lesson does not pretend these terms have accepted operational meanings when they don't. START-I verification analogy holds up (on-site inspections, National Technical Means). Bletchley Declaration was signed by 28 states plus the EU, worth naming precisely rather than 'endorsed by 50+ nations' which is a summit-attendee figure blended in from the Political Declaration.
Gemini.topIssue: The '50+ nations' figure combines Political Declaration signatories with Bletchley Summit attendees — these are two different documents with different signatory counts.

Perplexity.notes: Bletchley (Nov 2023) and SF US-China talks (Nov 2023) are current. Missing: AI Seoul Summit (May 2024) and its Frontier AI Safety Commitments, the AI Action Summit in Paris (Feb 2025) with its divergence from the Bletchley approach, and the November 2024 US-China readout that dropped the 'no AI in nuclear command' language. The compute-governance discussion should reference the RAND / GovAI 2024 papers that gave the idea operational shape.
Perplexity.topIssue: The multilateral timeline stops at Bletchley 2023 — Seoul 2024 and Paris 2025 changed the coalition math and the lesson should reflect that.

Claude.notes: The Fouchier/Kawaoka H5N1 opening is the strongest single narrative move in the course — it lets the DURC framework emerge from a specific documented dilemma rather than being defined into existence. Collaborations Pharmaceuticals' MegaSyn re-tasking is used exactly as it should be: not as a scare story but as a demonstration that the uplift concept has operational teeth. The four-module lattice of biology → cyber → autonomy → governance holds together.
Claude.topIssue: L1's narrative-density is very high (the story runs long); an Advanced learner is still with you, but the balance is closer to 40% than the 20-35% target.

Gemini.notes: Technically the strongest module. DURC, uplift, infohazard, gain-of-function, de novo protein design (RFdiffusion), P3CO, and BLAST-based synthesis screening are all defined with the precision a working biosecurity researcher would recognize. Collaborations Pharmaceuticals (Urbina et al., Nature Machine Intelligence 2022) is correctly framed as a proof-of-concept, not an operational attack. EO 14110's Section 4.4 language on nucleic-acid synthesis screening aligns with what the module reports.
Gemini.topIssue: EO 14110 was largely rescinded by EO 14179 (January 2025); the biosecurity-screening substance was preserved in NIST/HHS follow-on guidance, but the citation should reflect the change.

Perplexity.notes: WormGPT/FraudGPT, UK AISI (2023), and Collaborations Pharmaceuticals (2022) are current touchstones. Missing: UK AISI's rename to AI Security Institute (Feb 2025) and its bilateral MOUs with US AISI; the January 2025 rescission of EO 14110; the RAND-BWC 2024 report on AI-assisted bioweapons uplift studies (which found modest uplift over baseline internet access) — that finding is directly relevant to the 'uplift' concept the module centers.
Perplexity.topIssue: The RAND 2024 AI-bioweapons uplift study (finding modest but non-zero uplift) is the most-cited recent empirical result on this exact question and is missing.
